scenes.line1: Why do types work by shape?
scenes.say: Ever wonder why TypeScript lets you assign one object type to another, even if their names don't match? Let's see why structure matters more than labels.

scenes.label: Shape
scenes.sub: TypeScript checks type compatibility by structure.
scenes.say: TypeScript uses structural typing. That means it checks if the actual properties and methods match, not the type's name.
Interfaces and type aliases can both describe shapes. But interfaces are for objects and can be extended or merged. Type aliases are more flexible, but can't be merged.
Here, an interface and a type alias both have a single number property. You can assign one to the other because their shapes match. The names don't matter.

scenes.question: Does TypeScript require type names to match?
scenes.right: No, only the structure must match
scenes.say: A common trap: thinking TypeScript cares about type names. It doesn't. Only the structure counts.
